steps.name: prompt
steps.text: Write the introduction for our paper on curiosity-driven red teaming of LLMs: explain why automated RL-based red teaming finds too narrow a set of test cases, and how optimizing for novelty fixes this, with a summary of our results.

steps.name: skeleton_outline
steps.text:
- LLMs succeed but can generate harmful content; hard to find triggering prompts
- Filtering outputs at deployment is impractical; test before deployment
- Red teaming, human and automated with RL
- RL red teaming lacks diversity -> low coverage
- Diversity tricks are not enough; optimize novelty (curiosity)
- Evaluation and findings

steps.name: detailed_outline
steps.text:
- Problem
  - LLMs: success in question-answering, virtual assistance, summarization, other NLP applications
  - big issue: misinformation and harmful content
  - millions / billions of parameters -> hard to inspect which prompts trigger unwanted text (toxic, hateful, untruthful)
- Filtering vs testing
  - classifier to filter output: needs multiple generations during deployment, computationally expensive
  - maybe no output passes
  - better: test before deployment, fine-tune to reduce undesired responses
- Red teaming
  - human testers design test cases (prompts) eliciting unwanted responses = red teaming / red teams
  - costly, time-consuming -> automate with red-team LLM (different from target) trained by RL
  - reward function scores undesirability of response; red-team LLM = policy generating prompts that elicit reward-maximizing responses
  - ideal: find all effective test cases
- Coverage problem
  - RL methods find effective test cases but lack diversity -> low coverage
  - target LLM not thoroughly evaluated, many triggering prompts missed
  - reason: only maximize reward, no incentive to span all test cases; converge to deterministic policy after a few effective cases
- Diversity vs novelty
  - common: higher sampling temperature of the policy, entropy bonus in RL objective
  - we found diversity only minimally increases coverage (Section 4.5)
  - directly optimize novelty: curiosity-driven exploration, jointly maximize novelty and task reward
  - novelty via text similarity metrics; lower similarity to past test cases = higher novelty
- Evaluation
  - curiosity-driven red teaming (CRT); text continuation and instruction following
  - higher coverage than current RL red teaming
  - effectiveness = toxicity of elicited responses (prevalent in red teaming; method works for any metric)
  - curiosity also improves effectiveness
  - finds toxic prompts even for LLMs fine-tuned with a few rounds of RLHF -> current RLHF insufficient
  - curiosity likely vital for automated red teaming

steps.name: partial_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) have had unprecedented success in question-answering, virtual assistance, summarization, and other applications of natural language processing (NLP). One big issue when deploying LLMs is that they can generate misinformation and harmful content. But LLMs often have several millions or billions of parameters, so it is challenging to inspect which prompts make an LLM produce unwanted text (e.g., toxic, hateful, or untruthful).

One option is to use a classifier to filter the output of the LLM so that the user does not see unwanted responses. However, this approach is usually infeasible, because during deployment it needs multiple generations from the LLM to find an output that passes the filter, which is computationally expensive. Also, it is possible that even after multiple generations no output passes the classifier. So instead of filtering during deployment, it is ideal to test the LLM before deployment and fine-tune it to reduce the chance of undesired responses during deployment.

Right now, models are tested by human testers who design test cases (i.e., prompts) that elicit unwanted responses from the target LLM. This paradigm is called red teaming, and the human testers are called red teams. Human red teaming is costly and time-consuming, so a promising alternative is to automate the generation of test cases with a red-team LLM (which is a different model than the target LLM) using reinforcement learning (RL). If we have a reward function that can score how undesirable the generated response is, the red-team LLM can be seen as a policy trained with RL to generate prompts for the target LLMs that elicit responses that maximize the reward. An ideal method for automatic red-teaming would find all test cases (or prompts) that are effective, i.e., that elicit an unwanted response from the target LLM.

Existing RL-based methods for automatic red teaming do find effective test cases, but the test cases they generate lack diversity, and this gives low coverage of the span of prompts that elicit undesirable responses. Insufficient coverage means the target LLM is not thoroughly evaluated, since many prompts that can trigger unwanted responses are missed. The main reason for the low coverage is that current RL methods are only trained to maximize rewards (i.e., generate effective test cases) and have no incentive to span all possible test cases. After a few effective test cases are found, RL training reinforces these few test cases to get high rewards and quickly converges to a deterministic policy. So RL approaches overlook alternative test cases that are equally effective, and the coverage of effective test cases is low.

- Diversity vs novelty
  - usual tricks: higher sampling temperature of the policy, entropy bonus in RL objective
  - we found diversity barely increases coverage (Section 4.5)
  - optimize novelty directly: curiosity-driven exploration, novelty + task reward jointly
  - novelty from text similarity metrics; lower similarity = higher novelty
- Evaluation
  - CRT on text continuation and instruction following; higher coverage than RL red teaming
  - effectiveness = toxicity of elicited responses (common in red teaming; any metric works)
  - curiosity also improves effectiveness
  - finds toxic prompts even against LLMs fine-tuned with a few rounds of RLHF -> RLHF insufficient
  - curiosity likely vital for automated red teaming

steps.name: rough_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) have had unprecedented success in question-answering, virtual assistance, summarization, and other applications of natural language processing (NLP). One big issue when deploying LLMs is that they can generate misinformation and harmful content. But LLMs often have several millions or billions of parameters, so it is challenging to inspect which prompts make an LLM produce unwanted text (e.g., toxic, hateful, or untruthful).

One option is to use a classifier to filter the output of the LLM so that the user does not see unwanted responses. However, this approach is usually infeasible, because during deployment it needs multiple generations from the LLM to find an output that passes the filter, which is computationally expensive. Also, it is possible that even after multiple generations no output passes the classifier. So instead of filtering during deployment, it is ideal to test the LLM before deployment and fine-tune it to reduce the chance of undesired responses during deployment.

Right now, models are tested by human testers who design test cases (i.e., prompts) that elicit unwanted responses from the target LLM. This paradigm is called red teaming, and the human testers are called red teams. Human red teaming is costly and time-consuming, so a promising alternative is to automate the generation of test cases with a red-team LLM (which is a different model than the target LLM) using reinforcement learning (RL). If we have a reward function that can score how undesirable the generated response is, the red-team LLM can be seen as a policy trained with RL to generate prompts for the target LLMs that elicit responses that maximize the reward. An ideal method for automatic red-teaming would find all test cases (or prompts) that are effective, i.e., that elicit an unwanted response from the target LLM.

Existing RL-based methods for automatic red teaming do find effective test cases, but the test cases they generate lack diversity, and this gives low coverage of the span of prompts that elicit undesirable responses. Insufficient coverage means the target LLM is not thoroughly evaluated, since many prompts that can trigger unwanted responses are missed. The main reason for the low coverage is that current RL methods are only trained to maximize rewards (i.e., generate effective test cases) and have no incentive to span all possible test cases. After a few effective test cases are found, RL training reinforces these few test cases to get high rewards and quickly converges to a deterministic policy. So RL approaches overlook alternative test cases that are equally effective, and the coverage of effective test cases is low.

One way to increase coverage is to increase the diversity of the output of the policy. It is common to increase the diversity of LLM outputs by increasing the sampling temperature of the policy and adding an entropy bonus to the RL training objective. However, we found that diversity only increases coverage minimally. A small set of dissimilar test cases is diverse (i.e., maximizes entropy), but it may not cover the span of all possible effective test cases (see discussion in Section 4.5).

A more direct way to increase coverage is to optimize for the novelty of the generated test cases directly. In this form, the problem of finding effective test cases that increase coverage can be cast into the curiosity-driven exploration framework, where we jointly maximize the novelty and the task reward. We measure the novelty of test cases with text similarity metrics. Lower similarity to previously generated test cases means higher novelty.

We evaluate our curiosity-driven red teaming (CRT) method on text continuation and instruction following scenarios. The evaluation shows that the proposed method (CRT) increases the coverage of the generated tests compared to current RL-based red-teaming methods. We measure the effectiveness of test cases as the toxicity of the responses elicited from the target LLM. We use toxicity as a metric because it is prevalent in red teaming, but our method can be applied to any other metric. Interestingly, curiosity-driven exploration also improves the effectiveness of red teaming, which implies that better exploration lets a red-team model discover more effective test cases. We show that CRT can find prompts that elicit toxic responses even from LLMs that were fine-tuned with a few rounds of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF). These results show both that our method is useful and that the current RLHF methods are not enough to make LLMs safe. Our results also suggest that curiosity-driven exploration is likely to be a vital component for effective automated red teaming.

steps.name: revised_draft
steps.text:
Large language models (LLMs) have achieved unprecedented success in question-answering, virtual assistance, summarization, and other applications of natural language processing (NLP). A big issue in deploying LLMs is the potential generation of misinformation and harmful content [1]. However, since LLMs often consist of several millions or billions of parameters, inspecting which prompts trigger an LLM to produce unwanted text (e.g., toxic, hateful, or untruthful) is challenging.

One possibility is to use a classifier to filter the LLM's output so that a user is not presented with unwanted responses. However, such an approach is usually infeasible, as it requires multiple generations from the LLM during deployment to find an output that passes the filtering – a computationally expensive process. Further, it is possible that no output passes the classifier despite multiple generations. Therefore, instead of filtering during deployment, it is ideal to test the LLM before deployment and fine-tune it to reduce the chances of undesired responses during deployment.

Currently, models are tested by human testers who design test cases (i.e., prompts) that elicit unwanted responses from the target LLM [2]. This paradigm is called red teaming, and the human testers are called red teams. As human red teaming is costly and time-consuming, a promising alternative is to automate test case generation using a red-team LLM [3] (a different model than the target LLM) trained with reinforcement learning (RL) [4]. Assuming access to a reward function that can score the undesirability of the generated response, the red-team LLM can be thought of as a policy trained via RL to generate prompts for the target LLMs that elicit reward-maximizing responses. An ideal method for automatic red-teaming would identify all test cases (or prompts) that are effective – i.e., that elicit an unwanted response from the target LLM.

Existing RL-based methods for automatic red teaming identify effective test cases, but the generated test cases lack diversity, resulting in low coverage of the span of prompts that elicit undesirable responses. Insufficient coverage means that the target LLM is not thoroughly evaluated, as many prompts that can trigger unwanted responses are missed. The primary reason for the low coverage is that current RL methods are only trained to maximize rewards (i.e., generate effective test cases) without any incentive to span all possible test cases. Once a few effective test cases are found, RL training reinforces these few test cases to obtain high rewards and quickly converges to a deterministic policy [5,6]. Thus, RL approaches overlook alternative but equally effective test cases, resulting in low coverage of effective test cases.

One way to increase coverage is to increase the diversity of the policy's output. It is common to increase the diversity of LLM outputs by increasing the sampling temperature [7] of the policy [8] and adding an entropy bonus [9] to the RL training objective. However, we found that diversity only minimally increases coverage – a small set of dissimilar test cases is diverse (i.e., maximizes entropy), but may not cover the span of all possible effective test cases (see discussion in Section 4.5).

A more direct way to increase coverage is to directly optimize for the novelty of the generated test cases. In this form, the problem of finding effective test cases that increase coverage can be cast into the curiosity-driven exploration framework [14,15,16] of jointly maximizing novelty and task reward. We measure the novelty of test cases using text similarity metrics [17,18], where lower similarity to previously generated test cases indicates higher novelty.

We evaluate our curiosity-driven red teaming (CRT) method on text continuation and instruction following scenarios. The evaluation reveals that CRT increases the coverage of the generated tests compared to current RL-based red-teaming methods. The effectiveness of test cases is measured as the toxicity of the responses elicited from the target LLM. We use toxicity as a metric because of its prevalence in red teaming [3], but our method can be applied to any other metric. Intriguingly, curiosity-driven exploration also improves the effectiveness of red teaming, implying that improved exploration enables a red-team model to discover more effective test cases. We show that CRT can successfully find prompts that elicit toxic responses even from LLMs that have been fine-tuned with a few rounds of reinforcement learning from human feedback (RLHF) [13]. These results highlight both the usefulness of our method and the fact that current RLHF methods are insufficient to make LLMs safe. Our results also indicate that curiosity-driven exploration is likely to be a vital component of effective automated red teaming.
